verses.translation_literal: Bless, my soul, [obj] YHWH. YHWH my God, you have become great exceedingly; splendor and majesty you have put on.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless the LORD, O my soul. LORD, my God, you are so great that the word itself is too small. You have dressed yourself in splendor; you wear majesty like a robe.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with the singer talking to himself: 'my soul' (nefesh) is, literally, the throat, the breathing, hungry self, and it is ordered to bless. Play it as a man rousing himself before a great sight, not as a calm hymn. The KJV's 'Bless the Lord, O my soul' is right, but its 'thou art clothed with honour and majesty' turns an active verb into a state: lavashta is 'you have put on', a deliberate act of dressing. Hod and hadar ('splendor and majesty') are the vocabulary of kings, the glory of a court, so God is a king who has chosen his robes, and the whole psalm will go on to show what the robes are made of. 'Great' (gadalta) is a verb too, 'you have grown great', and 'exceedingly' (me'od) pushes it to the limit.

In a world of kingdoms where a ruler was known by his regalia, the picture is concrete: the audience would think of a throne room, not of an idea.

philological_notes.note: Not 'soul' in the Greek sense: nefesh is the throat and breath, the whole living self with its appetites. The speaker commands his own life to bless.
A pair for royal splendor, used of kings and of God as king. Radak reads it as the heavenly spheres God made first, which a man sees as one sees a king's robe and so knows the king.

verses.translation_literal: Wrapping himself [in] light like a garment, stretching out [the] heavens like a tent-curtain.
verses.translation_dramatic: He wraps himself in light as a man throws a cloak about his shoulders, and he draws the heavens out wide, as a tent is drawn open for the night.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice shifts from 'you' to 'he': the singer turns from God to the world and speaks about him. The picture is a shepherd's: a cloak thrown on, a tent pulled out. 'Light' is the garment, which is why no one sees God, only what covers him; Malbim makes just this point about light hiding the one who wears it. The KJV 'coverest thyself' keeps the idea but 'curtain' loses the Hebrew yeri'ah, the word for the panels of tent cloth, the same word used for the curtains of the Tabernacle. So the sky is a tent being pitched, and the stretching of it is the verb nata, the verb of the tent-peg and the tent-line. The participles ('wrapping', 'stretching') are continuous: God is doing this now, every morning.

philological_notes.note: A panel of tent cloth, the word used for the Tabernacle's curtains; 'curtain' in the KJV is close but loses the nomad's tent.
To wrap oneself, to cloak. Meiri discusses whether it is related to natah 'stretch out' or is a root of its own, meaning 'clothe'.

verses.translation_literal: The one who beams his upper rooms in the waters, the one who sets clouds [as] his chariot, the one who walks upon the wings of wind.
verses.translation_dramatic: He lays the beams of his high chamber in the waters above, and builds his house where no hand can climb. He sets the clouds beneath him as a chariot, and rides. He walks upon the wings of the wind, and the whole sky bends and hurries under his tread.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three participles in a row, each ending a clause with the same stately cadence: the one who beams, the one who sets, the one who walks. Do not play them as three separate pictures. They are one hymn-like list of titles, and the voice should keep rising. The first image is architecture. A house in the ancient Near East was roofed with beams laid across the walls, and the 'upper room' (aliyah) was the cool, airy chamber on the flat roof, where a householder received an honoured guest (compare Elisha's room on the wall, 2 Kings 4:10). God's upper room is built on the waters, the heavenly ocean the ancient world imagined above the vault of the sky. Metzudat David and Malbim read it that way; Ibn Ezra takes the upper rooms to be the clouds themselves. Either way, the point is that the Creator's house rests on the very element that to Israel's neighbours meant chaos.

The KJV 'layeth the beams of his chambers' is serviceable, but it archaizes the 'upper rooms' into 'chambers', which loses the picture of a rooftop room, and it turns a verb into a noun phrase. The Hebrew has a verb built from the noun 'beam': he beams. Nehemiah 3:3 uses the same verb for roofing the Fish Gate, as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion note. The BBE, 'the arch of your house is based on the waters', changes both the image and the person.

The second line is polemic. Riding the clouds was the standing title of the storm-god of Canaan, Baal, 'rider of the clouds' in the Ugaritic texts. Here the title belongs to YHWH alone, and the clouds are not his weather but his vehicle. The word rekhuv is a chariot or mount, and Radak hears in it the cloud obeying its rider as a horse obeys its master. The KJV 'maketh the clouds his chariot' is faithful. The wind's wings, in the last line, are not a metaphor of speed alone: YHWH walks, not flies, on them, as a man on a road. Ibn Ezra reads speed; Malbim pictures the winds as the horses' wings drawing the chariot.

philological_notes.note: A participle of a denominative verb from qorah 'beam, rafter': 'the one who lays the beams'. The same verb is used of roofing a gate in Neh 3:3. The upper rooms are the object, not a possessive 'beams of'.
From 'alah 'go up': a room above, usually the rooftop chamber. It is the same word as in 2 Kings 4:10. 'Chambers' in the KJV hides the sense of height.
A rare noun for the thing one rides: a chariot or mount. The Ugaritic title of Baal, 'rider of the clouds', lies behind the polemic; the claim that the clouds are YHWH's is my own reading.

verses.translation_literal: Making his messengers winds, his servants a fire flaming.
verses.translation_dramatic: He makes the winds his messengers, and a flaming fire his servant.
verses.directors_commentary: Here two words in the verse are both ordinary and heavy: mal'akh is 'messenger', the same word that later becomes 'angel', and ruach is both 'wind' and 'spirit'. The KJV 'Who maketh his angels spirits' reads the verse the way Hebrews 1:7 quotes it, from the Greek, as a statement about the nature of angels. In the Hebrew, in this run of weather images, the more natural reading is that God sends wind and lightning as his errand-runners. Do not play it as a lesson in angelology; play it as a ruler who has only to lift a finger and the storm goes. 'Ministers' (meshartav) is the word for a servant in attendance, the one who stands in front of the master. 'Flaming' (lohet) is the vocabulary of fire licking up, used for flames that devour. Both words are in the plural for the servants and singular for the fire: one fire, many winds.

philological_notes.note: 'His messengers'. Whether the winds are the messengers or the messengers become winds depends on how the two objects are read; the Hebrew has no marker. Rashi and Radak take the winds as the messengers.

verses.translation_literal: He founded earth upon its foundations; it will not be shaken [for] ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: He set the earth on its footings, and it will not shake, not now, not ever.
verses.directors_commentary: The building image continues, but now we are below the roof: yasad is to lay a foundation, mekhonim are the bases or sockets, the place where a thing stands. The ancient listener lived with earthquakes, and with a picture of the earth as a structure standing on pillars over the deep; the line is a confession of trust. The KJV 'removed' is archaic; the verb is mot, 'to totter, to be shaken', the same verb the psalms use for the righteous who 'shall not be moved'. The negative bal is a poetic 'not' (used rarely in prose), heavier than lo, and gives the line a finality, a door closing. 'For ever and ever' is olam va'ed, literally 'age and beyond'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read this with Greek science as a sphere in the middle of the heavens; for the actors, the point is simpler: the ground under your feet is held.

philological_notes.note: A poetic negative, equivalent to 'not' but characteristic of verse; it appears again in verse 9 for the sea's boundary.
Foundations, bases (a place fixed to stand). Meiri notes the odd spelling, with a seghol under the nun.

verses.translation_literal: [The] deep, like clothing, you covered it; above [the] mountains stood [the] waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: You wrapped the earth in the deep, as in a cloak; the waters stood high above the mountains.
verses.directors_commentary: The song turns back to the beginning, to the world before dry land. The singer returns to the clothing image of verse 1, but now it is the earth that wears the garment, and the garment is the sea: tehom, 'the deep', is the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2. The word sounds like Babylonian Tiamat, the sea-goddess of the Babylonian creation epic, but here there is no goddess and no fight; the deep is simply a cloak laid on by God. That is the polemic: what other nations feared as a divine enemy is a piece of clothing. The KJV 'Thou coveredst it with the deep' supplies 'with', as Radak notes the Hebrew must; the Hebrew just puts 'the deep' first, like a stage direction. The 'it' is the earth (so Radak and Meiri). 'Stood' (ya'amdu) is a standing army's verb, a wall of water waiting for an order, which sets up the command of verse 7.

philological_notes.note: The deep, the primeval ocean (Genesis 1:2). Rashi equates it with the sea; Ibn Ezra with the deep place in the sea; Malbim with the earth beneath the waters.
'You covered it'. The suffix is masculine; Radak and Meiri explain that the earth, eretz, is treated as masculine in other places too.

verses.translation_literal: From your rebuke they flee; from [the] sound of your thunder they hurry away.
verses.translation_dramatic: At your rebuke they ran. At the sound of your thunder they scattered in a panic.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse where the waters, standing in verse 6, receive an order. Ga'arah is a rebuke, a shout at someone who is out of line; it is what God says to the sea elsewhere in the Bible, and a word you would use to a dog or a slave. The waters are not defeated: they are scolded, and they run. Ra'am is thunder, the voice of the storm-god again, here in God's mouth. The KJV 'hasted away' is the old-fashioned way to say what the Hebrew does with nifal chafaz: a hurried, frightened flight. The verbs are imperfect ('they flee') but describe a past event: the old way to tell a myth in the present tense, so that it becomes true every time it is told. Radak makes the same point, that a future form stands for the past. Delivery: the first half is a command, the second is the thunder behind it.

philological_notes.note: 'Your rebuke', a sharp word of correction, as to a subordinate. Rashi ties it to the word of Genesis 1:9, 'let the waters be gathered'.
They hurry away in alarm. Malbim distinguishes it from 'flee' (nus): the waters flee from a thing they must, and hurry toward a place they want.

verses.translation_literal: They went up [the] mountains, they went down [the] valleys, to [the] place that you had founded for them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Up over the mountains they went, and down into the valleys, to the place you had fixed for them.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a famous crux. It is either the waters which climb the hills and pour down the valleys until they reach their appointed basin (the KJV, Metzudat David, Radak) or it is the land which moves: mountains rise, valleys sink (the ASV in brackets and the BBE). The Hebrew is just four words, a chiasm, up-mountains, down-valleys, and does not say who is going. For the dramatic voice I have kept the waters as the subject, since they are the grammatical subject of verses 6 and 7. Yasad, 'founded', returns from verse 5: the place for the waters is a foundation too, a prepared basin, the sea-bed. God does not just drive the sea back; he has built a home for it first. 'Valleys' here is beqa'ot, wide plains between ranges, not the narrow wadis of verse 10.

philological_notes.note: Ambiguous: 'the mountains rose' or 'they [the waters] went up the mountains'. Metzudat David takes the waters as going against their nature, uphill, before descending.

verses.translation_literal: A boundary you set; they shall not cross over, they shall not return to cover the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: You drew a line, and they may not cross it; they shall not come back to bury the earth again.
verses.directors_commentary: God is the border guard of the sea: gevul is the boundary stone, a border marker whose moving was a crime in ancient law, and here the sea itself has one. Radak and Metzudat David say the border is the sand of the shore, as in Jeremiah 5:22, though the psalm does not name it. The double bal ('not... not') is a lock turned twice. The KJV 'that they may not pass over; that they turn not again' turns the Hebrew's flat promise into purposes, 'so that', and this softens a statement of what is: the waters will not return. The listener also knows the Flood, when they did return; a careful audience might hear the promise as a pointer to Genesis 9:11. Delivery: calm, with a shrug of authority; the sea is huge and the line is thin, and the line holds.

philological_notes.note: A boundary, border; Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David identify it with the sand around the sea's shore.

verses.translation_literal: The one who sends springs in the wadis; between [the] mountains they walk.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sends the springs into the dry stream-beds, and between the mountains the water walks.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood changes from battle to kindness. The sea was held back, and now God sends fresh water the other way, to the land. Nachal is not simply a 'valley' as in the KJV: it is a wadi, a dry stream-bed that runs only after rain, and a spring sent into one means a gift of permanent water in a thirsty place. This is how the audience, in a land of seasonal rivers, hears 'springs': life. 'They walk' (yehalekhun) uses the same verb as God walking on the wind in verse 3: the water has legs, and walks the same road as its maker. The KJV 'which run among the hills' is fine in sense; the Hebrew's 'walk' is quieter, a slow trickle, and the actors should slow down to it. Note the participle 'sending': it is an ongoing act, God as someone who turns on the water each day.

philological_notes.note: Wadis, seasonal stream-beds; 'valleys' of the KJV blurs this. Metzudat David notes that these are the streams whose water does not fail.

verses.translation_literal: They give drink [to] every living-thing of [the] field; wild donkeys break their thirst.
verses.translation_dramatic: They give drink to every creature of the open country, and the wild donkeys come and break their thirst.
verses.directors_commentary: The streams are the subject: they are the ones giving drink, not God directly, so the water is a host. Chayyat sadai is the 'living thing of the field', the wild animals of the open country as against the household ones. The wild donkey (pere') is the animal that stands for freedom and wasteland throughout the Bible: it is the one creature no man can tame (Job 39:5-8 is a hymn to him), and it is picked here because it lives farthest from people, as Radak and Meiri observe. The KJV 'wild asses' is correct; 'quench their thirst' softens the Hebrew, which says they break it, as one breaks a fast or breaks a bar: thirst is a thing with force, and the water snaps it. Ibn Ezra says it is a type for the animals in the desert of Kadesh; the reader should hear the whole wild.

philological_notes.note: 'They break their thirst': shavar is 'break', and the thirst is treated as something to be broken. Meiri glosses it 'satisfy themselves', and Metzudat David 'cancel the thirst'.
Wild donkeys, the free, untamed animal; Radak says they are named because they never come near settled land.

verses.translation_literal: Beside them the bird of the heavens dwells; from between [the] foliage they give [forth] voice.
verses.translation_dramatic: By these waters the birds of the sky make their home, and out of the leaves they lift their voice.
verses.directors_commentary: After the thirst of the animals, the sound: this is the first verse of the psalm that ends on a noise, not a picture. 'Beside them' (aleihem) means the springs and streams, as Rashi and Metzudat David say; the KJV 'By them shall the fowls... have their habitation' adds a future and a 'shall' that the Hebrew lacks, and 'fowls' is old for what we call birds, not poultry. 'Bird of the heavens' (of hashamayim) is a singular used for the whole flock, which is why the verb is singular first and plural after. The rare word 'ofa'im, foliage, is of Aramaic flavor (it appears in Daniel 4:9, as Rashi and Meiri note), and gives the line a bit of a rustle. The KJV 'sing among the branches' is lovely, but the Hebrew says, more plainly, they give voice: it can be song or just chatter. After the roars of thunder in verse 7, a small gentle sound should close this section.

philological_notes.note: Foliage, leaves; an Aramaic-looking word, found in Daniel 4:9 as 'afyeh. Rashi and Meiri point to Daniel; Ibn Ezra prefers 'leaves' to a rival view of 'branches'.

verses.translation_literal: Watering [the] mountains from his upper rooms, from [the] fruit of your works the earth is sated.
verses.translation_dramatic: And from his high rooms above the clouds he waters the mountains; the thirsty ridges drink, and the earth, fed from the fruit of your hands, is full.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet turns from the waters of the deep to water from above, and the change of address is abrupt: he speaks of God in the third person ("his upper rooms") and then speaks to him ("your works") in the same breath. Play it as a worshipper catching himself mid-sentence and turning to look at God.

The KJV's "chambers" is not wrong, but it hides that the word is the same 'aliyyah, a roof-chamber, that opened the psalm at v. 3: the Lord who laid the beams of his upper rooms on the waters now pours water down from them. The earth's "satisfied" is literally "sated", the verb of a full stomach, and the earth is eating the fruit of God's works. In a land with no great river, as in Canaan, where the crops lived or died by the autumn and winter rains, rain was not weather but a gift to be named. The ASV and BBE "filled" and "full" blunt this.

philological_notes.note: Upper rooms, the roof-chambers of a house, here the heavenly storehouses of rain; the commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David) identify them with the clouds. The same word appears in v. 3 of this psalm.
Is sated: the verb of eating one's fill. The earth is pictured as a guest at a feast.

verses.translation_literal: Causing grass to sprout for the beast, and vegetation for the labor of humankind, to bring forth bread from the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: He makes the grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the work of human hands, that bread may be drawn up out of the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two kinds of growth: the grass that grows without help, for the herd, and the plants that grow only when a person works them. The key phrase is "the labor of humankind", ʿavodat ha-adam. The Hebrew is the word for service, and it echoes Eden (Gen 2:5, "no man to till the ground"). The KJV's "for the service of man" sounds as if the plants serve humans; the Hebrew says that humans serve the plants, tilling them, and God gives bread through the work.

Lehem, "bread", is the staple: barley and wheat loaves eaten at every meal. The KJV's "food" is acceptable (the word can mean food in general), but "food" (so ASV too) loses the daily-bread image that v. 15 picks up.

philological_notes.note: For the labor/service of humankind. The noun is from the verb for working and serving; Radak reads it as the plants that need human tilling, in contrast to grass, which grows unaided.
Bread, and by extension food in general; Radak notes that bread stands for all food because it is the daily staple.

verses.translation_literal: And wine makes glad the heart of humankind, to make faces shine from oil, and bread sustains the heart of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: And wine, to gladden the heart of man; and oil, to make the face shine; and bread, to hold up the heart that would fail.
verses.directors_commentary:
The triad of grain, wine and oil is the Israelite larder, and the psalmist lines them up like three gifts laid on a table. Play it slow and warm: this is the feast, not the famine. "Heart" here is the whole inner person; wine gladdens it, bread props it up (the verb sa'ad means to support, to lean on, as in Gen 18:5, where Abraham offers a morsel of bread to "strengthen" the visitors' hearts).

The KJV's "oil to make his face to shine" puts a pronoun into the Hebrew, which has only "faces", plural, and "from oil". The phrase is deliberately vague: faces shine from oil rubbed on the skin (the usual reading), or from the oil's gift of a lamp, or from what oil makes possible; Radak and Meiri both debate it. The verb 'hatzhil', "make shine", belongs to a root that elsewhere means to neigh or cry out in joy (Isa 12:6), so a shining face is a face crying out for joy. Wine and bread are named twice with the same "heart of humankind", which closes the verse in a ring.

philological_notes.note: To make shine. The root also means to shout or neigh in joy (Isa 12:6), so the shining face is a rejoicing face. Metzudat Zion compares it with tzehalah, gladness (Esther 8).
To support, sustain; bread is what holds up the heart. Radak and Meiri cite Gen 18:5 and Judg 19:5, where the same verb is used for refreshing a guest with bread.

verses.translation_literal: They are sated, the trees of YHWH, the cedars of Lebanon which he planted.
verses.translation_dramatic: The trees of the LORD drink their fill, the cedars of Lebanon that his own hand planted.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the planted fields of men, the poet lifts his eyes to forest nobody planted. Lebanon's cedars, the tallest and most prized trees of the ancient Near East, were the timber of kings: Solomon's temple, Egyptian ships, Mesopotamian palaces. Here they are not timber but guests at the same feast, sated by the same rain. "Trees of YHWH" works as a superlative, "mighty trees", but Radak and Meiri hear it literally: these are the trees no human put in the ground.

The KJV's "full of sap" supplies a noun that is not there; the Hebrew simply says the trees are sated, the same verb as the earth in v. 13. The KJV also moves "which he hath planted" softly; the Hebrew points firmly at God as the gardener. Keep the verb 'he planted' strong: this is the only planting in the psalm that is God's.

philological_notes.note: Trees of YHWH: either a superlative, 'great trees' (compare 'cedars of God', Ps 80:11, so Meiri), or the trees that grow without human planting (Radak, Meiri).

verses.translation_literal: Which there birds nest; the stork, cypresses [are] her house.
verses.translation_dramatic: There the little birds build their nests, and the stork, high above them, makes her home in the cypress trees.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem narrows from forest to nest. The camera drops from the cedars to the birds in the branches, and then to one bird, the stork, named by the Hebrew with a pun: chasidah, "the faithful one", from chesed, loyalty. Large white storks nest in tall trees in Israel in the spring and autumn migration; Jeremiah 8:7 knows the stork's sense of its appointed times. The loyalty reading of the name is common, though nothing in the packet's commentaries states it.

The KJV "fir trees" is wrong: the Hebrew beroshim are cypresses or junipers, not fir. The Hebrew sentence also breaks off strangely: "the stork, cypresses are her house", a staccato phrase, which KJV smooths over with "as for the stork". Rashi hears the Deuteronomy 22:6 phrase for a bird's nest (qen tzippor) in the verb "nest", and Radak says the point is that even trees with no fruit serve the creatures who live in them.

philological_notes.note: The stork, from the root meaning loyalty or kindness; the standard identification is the white stork (BDB, HALOT). The name itself is the pun.
Cypresses or junipers; the KJV 'fir trees' is a mistranslation. Metzudat Zion calls it a tree that bears no fruit.
Make nests, from qen, a nest; Rashi links it to Deut 22:6, 'a bird's nest'.

verses.translation_literal: The mountains, the high [ones], [are] for the ibexes; crags [are] a refuge for the hyraxes.
verses.translation_dramatic: The high mountains belong to the wild goats, and the rocks are a hiding place for the hyrax.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now up the cliff face. The ibex is the sure-footed wild goat of the Judean wilderness and the Negev, seen by David in En-gedi (1 Sam 24:2); the shaphan, hyrax, is a small, fat, stout-limbed animal, rabbit-sized, that lives in rock crevices and whose only defense is a hole to dive into.

The KJV "conies" is an archaic word for rabbits, and it is wrong: the Hebrew shafan is the rock hyrax, which is not a rabbit or a rodent at all. BBE avoids the mistake only by saying "small beasts". "Wild goats" is acceptable, but the Hebrew ya'el is a specific animal. Note the structure of the verse: big animals get whole mountains, small ones get the crevices. Each creature has a place that fits it. Rashi gives the key sense of machseh: not just shelter but shade and hiding, as from a rainstorm.

philological_notes.note: Hyraxes (the rock hyrax); the KJV 'conies' (rabbits) misleads. The same animal appears in Lev 11:5, Prov 30:26.
Refuge, shelter; Rashi says it always means a shadow and hiding place, like cover from a flood or rain (Isa 25:4).

verses.translation_literal: He made [the] moon for appointed times; [the] sun knows its entering.
verses.translation_dramatic: He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows the hour of its going down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet turns from earth to the clock of the sky. The moon is first, because in Israel's calendar the month begins with the new moon and the day begins at sunset, so night, and the moon, come first. Mo'adim, the "appointed times", are the festivals and months: Passover and Tabernacles are fixed by the moon, and the Hebrew word is the same one used for the tent of meeting (ohel mo'ed). The KJV's "seasons" is too meteorological; these are meeting times, appointments with God.

The second half is a quiet image: the sun "knows" its entering. The Hebrew verb is yada', "to know", and the sun is almost a servant who knows his route. The KJV "going down" is fine, though the Hebrew word mavo means "entering", and the sun enters the west as one enters a house. Rashi (on Rosh Hashanah 25a) sets this against the moon, whose course varies, but note the verse does not say so.

philological_notes.note: Appointed times, set meetings: festivals and months. Rashi says the moon is for counting 'times and festivals'.
Its entering; for the sun this is its setting. Radak notes the word can cover both the rising and the setting.

verses.translation_literal: You set darkness, and it is night; in it creeps every animal of the forest.
verses.translation_dramatic: You lay down the darkness, and it is night; and in the night every beast of the forest stirs and creeps from its hiding.
verses.directors_commentary:
A hush. The poet turns to speak to God again, "you set darkness", and then the sentence breaks into a Genesis echo: "and it is night" (vi-hi layelah) sounds like "and there was light" (vi-hi or), run in reverse. The Creator speaks darkness as he once spoke light.

The verb rāmas, "creep", is the Genesis word for all things that move low on the ground (Gen 1:24-26). The KJV "creep forth" is fine; the BBE "come quietly out of their secret places" invents a motive the Hebrew does not give. The weird form chayto, "animal of", has an old ending (the final vav is a poetic vestige, so Radak and Ibn Ezra): it is not "his beast". Night, for an ancient audience, was dangerous: it belonged to lions and jackals, and the poet does not flinch from that.

philological_notes.note: To creep, move about low to the ground; the Genesis 1 word for creeping things. Metzudat Zion points to Gen 1:28 (the 'creeping' creatures).
Animal of; the final vav is an old construct ending and does not mean 'his'.

verses.translation_literal: The young lions [are] roaring for prey, and to seek from God their food.
verses.translation_dramatic: The young lions roar after their prey, asking God for their meat.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm does not hide the predators; it gives them a voice. The kefirim are young lions in their prime, not cubs, as the KJV's "young lions" suggests, but Radak says exactly that: those in their young manhood. Their roar becomes a prayer: they seek "from God" their food. The Hebrew has the verb baqesh, "to seek, to ask", and the preposition "from El", so the roar is a request. Meiri and Radak say this is figurative: God gives food to every living thing, and the lions' hunting is, so to speak, their asking.

The KJV's "seek their meat" is correct but "meat" is archaic for food. The Hebrew word is ochel, plain food. Everything in this verse should sound both terrifying and devout; the prey is on the table before the lion has opened its mouth.

philological_notes.note: Young lions, those in their prime, hunting but not yet full-grown; Radak says 'young lions'.
To seek/ask from God: the lions' hunting is described as a request. Radak and Meiri read it figuratively, as God giving food to all living things.

verses.translation_literal: The sun rises; they withdraw, and into their dens they lie down.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sun rises, and they slip away; back into their dens they sink and lie down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn is as sharp as a door closing. The sun comes up and the night shift goes off duty. The Hebrew is two short verbs with an old poetic ending (-un) that gives each a falling cadence: ye'asefun, yirbatzun. The first verb means "they are gathered", a passive sense, as if the light itself pulls them back into their lairs; KJV's "they gather themselves together" suggests a pack assembling, which is not the picture. They retreat, alone, to their dens.

The second verb, ravatz, is "to lie down" as a beast does: crouch, stretch out. Rashi and Radak both say they go to hiding because of people, who are now going out to work. This is not a verse about lions' dens only; it is an ordering of the day, in which the animals have the night and people have the day.

philological_notes.note: They withdraw, are gathered in; the niphal passive with the poetic -un ending. Metzudat David: they gather themselves to their hiding places.
They lie down, crouch as animals do; Metzudat Zion says it is the lying down to rest.

verses.translation_literal: Humankind goes out to his work, and to his labor until evening.
verses.translation_dramatic: And man goes out to his work, to his labor, and he keeps at it until the evening comes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The day shift arrives. The verse is plain and unhurried, almost a pause for breath after the lions: no verbs but one, "goes out", and a measured ending, "until evening". Ancient farmers and herders went out at sunrise and came back at dusk; there was no clock but the sun, and the hours of daylight were all the working hours there were. "Evening" (ʿerev) is the start of the next day for Israel, so the verse ends exactly where the night shift begins again.

The KJV "Man goeth forth" is fine, though the word adam is "humankind", not just men; in a village, women worked in the fields and at the grindstone. KJV and ASV echo the near-synonyms "work" and "labour" faithfully. Notice the pairing with v. 14: the same ʿavodah, the labor that coaxes bread from the earth, is the labor the person goes out to do.

philological_notes.note: To his labor, service; the same noun as 'the labor of humankind' in v. 14, so the work of the day is the work that brings forth bread.

verses.translation_literal: How many have been your works, YHWH! All of them in wisdom you have made; the earth is full of your possessions.
verses.translation_dramatic: How many are your works, O LORD! In wisdom you made them every one; the whole earth is full of what is yours.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, and the poet stops listing and just exclaims. "How!" (mah) opens as a cry, not a question; Metzudat Zion says mah here means exaggeration, as in "how great is your goodness" (Ps 31:20). Perform it as a deep breath after the long catalogue of rain, bread, cedars, ibexes, lions and workers.

The KJV "manifold" is a good word for rabbu, "they are many", but "riches" for qinyan is softer than the Hebrew: qinyan means property, what one has acquired. Rashi connects it with God as "owner (qoneh) of heaven and earth" (Gen 14:19), and Radak and Metzudat David both read "your possessions", all that fills the world belongs to you. The earth is not a wilderness or a gift to humans but God's estate, stocked with creatures. The KJV's "in wisdom hast thou made them all" is right: the Hebrew puts "all of them" before "in wisdom", so wisdom is the point of the sentence. Wisdom (chokhmah) is the quality by which, in Proverbs 3:19, YHWH "founded the earth".

philological_notes.note: Your possessions, your acquisitions; the root is the same as 'creator/owner (qoneh) of heaven and earth' in Gen 14:19. Rashi says it is everything that belongs to you. STEPBible's 'creatures' is an interpretation.
With wisdom; wisdom is the means by which each work is fitted to its place, as Malbim says in explaining how the creatures are provided for.

verses.translation_literal: This [is] the sea, great and wide of hands; there [are] creeping things, and no number [to them], living things small with great.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there lies the sea, vast, spread wide on every hand, its far edges out of sight. Beneath its surface a world is crawling and darting and drifting, more than any mouth could count: the small beside the great, all of them alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet turns from land to water and points, as if the actors are standing on a shore: zeh, "this" sea. For an Israelite the Mediterranean is the edge of the known world, the home of chaos in Canaanite myth, where Yamm is the god of the sea. Here it is simply a big, crowded house. "Wide of hands" is a literal Hebrew idiom for roomy: hands as the reach of the arms on either side. Rashi glosses it as simply "wide of place," and Metzudat Zion reads yadayim as "place."

The KJV "things creeping innumerable" is close, but "beasts" for chayot is a stretch: the word is the ordinary "living things" and covers fish, eels and whales. Remes, "creeping/moving thing," is the same word Genesis 1 uses for what crawls on land and swarms in the water. The verse thus carries the creation of the fifth day: Radak says it speaks of "the sea creatures, created on the fifth day." Notice the pair "small with great": no hierarchy, they live together. Malbim adds that the numbers are beyond count because fish breed in millions.

philological_notes.note: A moving, swarming or creeping creature; in Genesis 1 the word covers what moves on the ground and in water. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a word of movement. Here it names the swarming life of the sea.
Literally "wide of hands," an idiom for spacious, broad on every side. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read yadayim as "place, room."

verses.translation_literal: There ships go about; Leviathan, [this one] you formed to play in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: There the ships pass back and forth over the deep. And there is Leviathan, the monster you shaped, loosed in these waters to play.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two things share the same sea: human ships and the monster of myth. The Israelites were no sailors; their sea-going neighbours the Phoenicians were, so ships here are a marvel. Metzudat David and Radak call them a wonder of God, who put wisdom into human minds to cross where no one can live.

Then the sting: Leviathan, in Canaanite poetry (Ugarit's Litan) the many-headed enemy of the storm god, and in Isaiah 27:1 a beast the LORD will slay. Here he is a creature the LORD "formed," yatsar, the potter's verb, "to play." The whole mythology of chaos is deflated in one line. Whether the play is Leviathan's or God's is left open by the suffix: Rashi, citing the Talmud (Avodah Zarah 3b) and Job 40:29, says God plays with him three hours a day. The KJV "that leviathan" and "play therein" keep the first reading; BBE's "plaything" takes the second. Do not play him as terror: he is a whale of a toy.

philological_notes.note: The sea monster, known from Ugaritic as Litan and from Job 3:8, 40:25 and Isaiah 27:1. Ibn Ezra takes it as a name for a great fish or a whole species. Here the myth is made a creature that God formed.
"To play, laugh, sport." The suffix can be "in it" (the sea) or "with him" (Leviathan); the rabbis read it as God playing with Leviathan.

verses.translation_literal: All of them to you they wait, to give their food in its time.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every one of them, the great and the small, lifts its waiting toward you: look to you for food, and look for it in its season.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera pulls back from the sea to the whole living world, and the mood changes from wonder to dependence. Every creature is a beggar at a door. "Wait" is sabar, "to look hopefully," the same verb the Metzudat Zion ties to "hope in the LORD" in Psalm 146. This is not passive: it is the posture of an animal watching a hand. In a land that lives on seasonal rain, "in its time" (be'ito) is a confession of how fragile the harvest is. If the rain is late, nobody eats.

The KJV "meat" is archaic: it means food in general, not flesh. The Hebrew also uses a singular suffix, "its time," which Radak reads as each kind having its own season. The verse recalls Psalm 145:15 in tone. Ibn Ezra says "all of them" includes the sea creatures just mentioned: even Leviathan's meal is provided.

philological_notes.note: To look with hope, to wait expectantly; a different root from the common "break." Metzudat Zion ties it to "hope in the LORD."

verses.translation_literal: You give to them, they gather; you open your hand, they are satisfied [with] good.
verses.translation_dramatic: You give, and they gather what you give. You open your hand, and they are filled with good things.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two clauses, two gestures, in perfect parallel: the giving and the gathering, then the open hand and the full belly. Play it as one slow movement: a hand lowering, then opening wide.

The verbs do not match in size. Ilqotun, "they gather," is the word for gleaning the leftover grain in the fields (Ruth 2): small, scattered, picked up bit by bit. Yisbe'un tov, "are satisfied with good," is a feast. Radak and Metzudat David both read the two lines as two conditions: sometimes God gives sparingly and creatures glean, sometimes the hand opens wide and they are sated. Meiri takes it more gently: God provides so that they need not even search. The KJV "they are filled with good" fits; "that thou givest them they gather" is clumsy because it makes the first half a relative clause the Hebrew does not have.

philological_notes.note: To gather, glean, pick up piece by piece; the word of the poor in the field (Ruth 2). Radak and Metzudat David take it as the sparse times when creatures only gather a little.

verses.translation_literal: You hide your face, they are dismayed; you gather in their breath, they expire, and to their dust they return.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then you turn your face away, and they are seized by panic. You draw their breath back into yourself, and they sink, one by one, and go home to the dust they were taken from.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm. For twenty-eight verses every creature has waited on the open hand; here the hand closes, and the verse is built to feel it. Each clause is two beats, a divine act and a creaturely response, with no connecting word between them: you hide, they are dismayed; you gather, they expire. Nothing intervenes between God's act and the creature's collapse. Play it as cause and effect without a pause.

The 'hiding of the face' is the opposite of the face that gives life elsewhere in the Psalter. In this psalm it has a concrete meaning, which Radak spells out as withholding food: when you hide your face, the creatures lose their feed and are left without help. Ibn Ezra reads it as God seeming not to see them, and Metzudat David as the moment the face is hidden completely, when panic takes hold. The verb yibahelun is a sudden, bodily alarm, a startle, not a settled mood. The KJV's 'troubled' is too mild and too reflective; the Hebrew is closer to 'they are thrown into a panic'.

The verb tosef is the verse's real puzzle. The form looks as if it came from yasaf, 'to add', which would make no sense. Radak, Meiri and the Metzudot read it as a form of asaf, 'gather', as if it said te'esof, and Meiri compares the form vayosef in 'and David again gathered' (2 Sam 6:1). On that reading God gathers the breath back to himself, the reverse of the giving in the next verse, where it is sent out. Rashi takes it differently, as 'ending, being finished', in the sense of Ps 73:19, 'they are finished, they are done'. Both readings leave the same picture, the breath going out and not coming back. The KJV 'takest away' turns the image of gathering into plain removal. The Hebrew breath here is ruach, the same word as 'spirit' and 'wind', so the death is also a recall of the wind that gave life.

The last clause turns to Genesis: 'to their dust they return' echoes Genesis 3:19. The KJV's 'return to their dust' reads smoothly, but the Hebrew puts the destination first, 'and to their dust', as the final, unavoidable place. The verbs are all plural and all imperfect: this is not one death but what happens to every creature, at every moment.

philological_notes.note: Read as a variant of te'esof 'you gather', from asaf, with the aleph dropped, rather than from yasaf 'add'. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion say it stands for te'esof; Meiri compares vayosef in 2 Sam 6:1. Rashi instead understands it as 'ending, being finished', like safu tammu in Ps 73:19.

Niphal of bahal, 'to be dismayed, thrown into sudden alarm'. It describes a startled, physical reaction. The long ending -un is a poetic form of the plural imperfect, shared by the verbs yigva'un and yeshuvun in the same verse.

verses.translation_literal: You send out your spirit, they are created; and you renew the face of the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then you send out your breath, and they are made: new life where there was none. And the face of the ground is renewed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The great reversal. The same ruach that was gathered in v.29 is now sent out. The speaker turns the cycle of death into a new creation: not one act at the beginning of time, but every spring, every birth. The verb is bara, "create," the verb reserved in Genesis 1 for God, here in a passive form, "they are created."

The KJV "face of the earth" is fine, but the Hebrew word is adamah, "ground," the red soil from which Adam was formed. The ground has a face that God has seen and can renew: skin, like a person. Readers have taken this in two ways. Rashi and the Targum, which has "your holy spirit," and Radak's first reading, find resurrection of the dead. Radak's second reading, and Meiri's, find the endless renewal of generations: the individual dies, the species lives. Ibn Ezra notes that these two views were already argued by philosophers. Leave it open on stage: the actor should sound as if the poet does not yet know which.

philological_notes.note: "They are created"; passive of bara, the creation verb of Genesis 1. Ibn Ezra hints that those created are "others," new individuals, not the same ones.
Breath, wind or spirit; the same word as "their breath" in v.29. The Targum makes it "your holy spirit."

verses.translation_literal: May the glory of YHWH be for ever; may YHWH rejoice in his works.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the glory of the LORD last for ever. Let the LORD take joy in what his hands have made.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm shifts from description to wish. Both verbs are jussive: "may it be," "may he rejoice." The KJV "shall endure ... shall rejoice" turns a prayer into a forecast, and the ASV and BBE are closer. This is a congregation speaking, almost a blessing over the world it has just seen.

God rejoicing in his works is the psalm's answer to Genesis 1, where each day ends "it was good": the creator enjoys what he made. It also quietly answers the tragic note of Genesis 6:6, where God was grieved at his making; Meiri and Metzudat David both set the two against each other, and Radak adds that joy and sorrow are said of God only by analogy. Ibn Ezra says the glory of the LORD is the creatures themselves.

philological_notes.note: Jussive of "be": "let there be, may it be," the same form as "let there be light" in Genesis 1:3. A wish, not a statement.

verses.translation_literal: The one who looks to the earth, and it trembles; he touches the mountains, and they smoke.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has only to look at the earth, and it shakes. He has only to touch the mountains, and they pour out smoke.
verses.directors_commentary:
A sudden, awful picture: God's gaze alone makes the ground shudder. The participle "the one who looks" turns it into a name for him. Compare the Sinai scene Rashi cites, Exodus 19:18, where the mountain "smoked, all of it." This is the poet's counterweight to the gentleness of the previous lines: the same hand that opens to feed can touch, and the world burns.

For a Judean audience the images are real: earthquakes along the Rift Valley, and the smoke of fire and storm on the hills. The KJV "hills" understates harim, which are mountains, and "he toucheth" is correct. Radak notes that "touch" and "look" are the same thing: his notice is his action. Ibn Ezra, in contrast, reads this as the world's stability: only his will keeps it from quaking.

philological_notes.note: "And they smoke"; the verb is built from the noun "smoke" and is used of Sinai in Exodus 19:18, which Rashi cites.

verses.translation_literal: I will sing to YHWH in my life; I will make music to my God in my continuing.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will sing to the LORD as long as I have life. I will make music to my God for as long as I am.
verses.directors_commentary:
The "I" enters at last, after thirty-two verses about the world. The speaker answers the vision with a vow, in two lines that say the same thing twice: "in my life" and "in my still-being." Metzudat David notes the doubling. The two verbs, shir and zamar, are "sing" and "sing with an instrument": voice and strings together.

The KJV "as long as I live ... while I have my being" is a good rendering, if stiff. What the Hebrew adds is the word od, "yet, still": be'odi means "in my still-being," as long as I am yet here. It is the same word Rashi finds in Deuteronomy 31:27, "while I am still alive." The vow is made in the face of v.29: the singer knows that breath is on loan, and promises to spend it on song.

philological_notes.note: "In my still-being, while I am yet." Rashi compares Deuteronomy 31:27.

verses.translation_literal: May my meditation be sweet to him; I, I will rejoice in YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: May what I murmur in my heart be sweet to him. As for me, I will rejoice in the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet, almost shy line. Siach, "meditation," is muttering, thinking aloud, the low sound of someone talking to themselves in prayer: Metzudat Zion glosses it as "speech." The KJV "my meditation of him" is vague. The Hebrew says "my meditation on him," and a better sense is "may it please him." Ya'arav, "be sweet," has the sense of being pleasant on the tongue; Metzudat Zion compares the offering that is "pleasing to the LORD" in Malachi 3:4.

The poet's pair in v.31, "may YHWH rejoice," is answered here, "I, I will rejoice," with the pronoun anokhi doubled for emphasis: Ibn Ezra says it is in answer to the verse about God's joy. God rejoices in his works; the poet rejoices in God. Let the actor lean on the repeated "I."

philological_notes.note: Meditation, musing, speech; Metzudat Zion glosses it as "my speaking."
To be sweet, pleasing; Metzudat Zion ties it to the sweetness of an offering in Malachi 3:4.

verses.translation_literal: May sinners be finished from the earth, and wicked [ones] be no more. Bless YHWH, my soul. Praise Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let sinners come to an end upon the earth, and the wicked be no more. Bless the LORD, O my soul. Praise the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sudden, hard wish at the end of a gentle psalm is one of the oldest puzzles in Psalms. After a vision of the world held in God's hand, the poet asks that those who spoil it be removed. It is not a battle cry, but a wish for a clean world: Metzudat David reads it as a prayer that people overcome their impulses, so that there would be no wicked left. Ibn Ezra reads it as the contrast to the singer's joy: sinners cannot take part in the praise.

The Talmud (Berakhot 10a, cited by Rashi) reads the first word as "sins" (chata'im) rather than "sinners," so that the prayer is that sins end, not people. The KJV "consumed" is a good sense for yitammu, "be finished, be complete," the root of tam, "whole": their account is wholly closed. Notice that "praise Yah" is the first Hallelujah in the whole Psalter: the KJV's "Praise ye the LORD" hides that it is one word with the short divine name Yah in it. The poet turns last to himself, "bless, my soul," the same refrain that opened the psalm.

philological_notes.note: "Let them be finished, brought to an end"; Metzudat Zion links it to tam, "complete." Jussive.
"Sinners," people who miss the mark. Rashi cites the Talmudic reading as "sins."
"Praise Yah": a plural command to praise, with the short form of the divine name. Radak explains the word as joining "praise" to "Yah" (half the Name).
